rows.notes: Capital offenses and any felony involving violence, serious injury or death have no time limit, so murder can be charged at any time.
Murder (and attempt, solicitation or conspiracy to commit murder) can be charged at any time.
Any homicide can be charged at any time.
Capital murder and first- and second-degree murder can be charged at any time.
Murder and other crimes punishable by death or life in prison can be charged at any time.
Murder (and kidnapping, treason, sex offenses against children and forgery) has no time limit.
Murder is a class A felony, and class A felonies can be charged at any time.
Murder and any class A felony (and attempts) can be charged at any time.
First- and second-degree murder, including murder of a police officer or public safety employee, can be charged at any time.
Capital felonies, life felonies and any felony that resulted in a death can be charged at any time.
Murder can be charged at any time.
Murder, attempted murder and conspiracy or solicitation to commit murder can be charged at any time.
Murder and voluntary manslaughter can be charged at any time.
First- and second-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder, involuntary manslaughter and reckless homicide can be charged at any time.
Murder can be charged at any time.
First- and second-degree murder can be charged at any time.
Capital murder and first- and second-degree murder can be charged at any time.
Kentucky has no time limit for any felony, including murder.
Crimes punishable by death or life in prison, which include first- and second-degree murder, can be charged at any time.
Murder and first- and second-degree criminal homicide can be charged at any time.
Maryland has no time limit for felonies, including murder; the limitations statute applies only to misdemeanors.
Murder can be charged at any time.
Murder, and conspiracy or solicitation to commit murder, can be charged at any time.
Any crime resulting in the victim's death can be charged at any time.
Murder and manslaughter can be charged at any time.
Murder and any class A felony can be charged at any time.
Deliberate, mitigated and negligent homicide can be charged at any time.
First-degree rape is a felony involving force, and those can be charged at any time. Any sex offense against a victim under 16 can also be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Lesser sex offenses against adults that do not involve violence fall under the 5-year felony period.

rows.notes: Sexual assault that is an unclassified, class A or class B felony (first- and second-degree) can be charged at any time. Felony sexual abuse of a minor can also be charged at any time.
Violent sexual assault and sexual assault (a class 2 felony sex offense) can be charged at any time, whatever the victim's age.

Rape of an adult must be charged within 6 years, but the limit is removed if biological evidence capable of producing a DNA profile of the perpetrator is identified. Rape of a minor can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; adult rape has 6 years unless DNA evidence exists.

rows.notes: Felony rape, sodomy, oral copulation and sexual penetration by force or similar means can be charged at any time if committed on or after January 1, 2017 or not yet time-barred then. The same applies to listed felony sex crimes against children.

Felony sexual assault of an adult must be charged within 20 years, with no limit if DNA identifies the suspect and the crime was reported within 20 years. Sex offenses against children can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; Colorado allows 20 years for adult felony sexual assault unless the DNA exception applies.

rows.notes: First-degree sexual assault and other class B-D felony sexual assaults of adults must be charged within 20 years; class A sexual assault has no limit. Sex offenses against minors have no limit, and victims aged 18-20 have until 30 years after they turn 21.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years; current law allows 20 years for felony sexual assault of an adult.

rows.notes: First-degree rape is a class A felony and can be charged at any time; lower degrees of rape against adults have 5 years, or 10 if based on DNA testing. Sexual offenses against minors can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Only first-degree rape has no limit for adult victims; second- through fourth-degree rape fall under the 5-year felony period.

rows.notes: First- through fourth-degree sexual abuse and all child sexual abuse offenses can be charged at any time.

First- or second-degree felony sexual battery of a victim 16 or older can be charged at any time if reported to police within 72 hours; otherwise within 8 years, with DNA-identification extensions. For victims under 18 the clock does not start until age 18, and sexual battery of a victim under 16 can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; the adult rule depends on reporting within 72 hours (no limit) or not (8 years).

rows.notes: Forcible rape must be charged within 15 years, but rape and aggravated sodomy can be charged at any time when DNA evidence establishes the accused's identity. Tolling and longer periods apply to child victims.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; forcible rape has 15 years unless DNA evidence identifies the accused.

rows.notes: First- and second-degree sexual assault can be charged at any time. For other felony sex offenses, the clock does not run while the victim is under 18.
Forcible rape (Idaho Code § 18-6101(3)-(10)) can be charged at any time. Sexual abuse of a child and lewd conduct with a child can also be charged at any time.
Criminal sexual assault, aggravated criminal sexual assault and any offense involving sexual penetration can be charged at any time. The same is true when the victim was under 18.

Level 3 felony rape must be charged within 5 years, or within 10 years after DNA evidence, a recording or a confession is discovered; Level 1 rape can be charged at any time. Listed sex crimes against children can be charged until the victim turns 31.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; only Level 1 and 2 felonies have no limit, and basic rape is a Level 3 felony.

rows.notes: First- to third-degree sexual abuse of an adult must be charged within 10 years, or within 3 years after a DNA profile identifies the suspect, whichever is later. If the victim was under 18, it can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; the no-limit rule applies only to victims under 18.

rows.notes: Rape and aggravated criminal sodomy can be charged at any time. Other sexually violent crimes have 10 years (adult victims) or 10 years after a child victim turns 18, with DNA extensions.
Rape is a felony, and Kentucky has no time limit for felonies. Misdemeanor sex offenses against minors have extended periods.

First-degree rape (punishable by life) and second-degree (forcible) rape can be charged at any time; other sex offenses can be charged within 3 years after DNA or new video identifies the offender. Sex offenses against minors have 30 years starting at the victim's 18th birthday.
rows.issue: Third-degree rape is not on the no-limit list and falls under the felony periods.

rows.notes: Class A, B and C gross sexual assault and unlawful sexual contact must be charged within 20 years. If the victim was under 18, rape and gross sexual assault can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; for adult victims Maine allows 20 years.

rows.notes: Rape is a felony, and Maryland has no time limit for felonies, whatever the victim's age.

Rape of an adult must be charged within 15 years. Rape and abuse of a child and other listed child sex crimes can be charged at any time, and the clock for a victim under 16 starts at age 16 or when reported.

First-degree criminal sexual conduct can be charged at any time. Second- and third-degree criminal sexual conduct has 15 years or until the victim's 42nd birthday, whichever is later, running from DNA identification if applicable.
rows.issue: Only first-degree CSC has no limit; third-degree CSC (forced penetration without aggravating factors) has the 15-year/age-42 period.

rows.notes: First- through fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct can be charged at any time, whatever the victim's age.
rows.issue: Value was 9 years; Minnesota removed the limit for first- to fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct.

rows.notes: Rape can be charged at any time, as can sexual battery of a child. Sexual battery of an adult has no limit only if DNA testing later identifies the accused; otherwise 2 years.
First-degree rape and forcible rape (and attempts) can be charged at any time, whatever the victim's age.

Sexual intercourse without consent and sexual assault of an adult must be charged within 10 years, or within 1 year after DNA testing identifies the suspect. If the victim was under 18, they can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; the no-limit rule applies only to victims under 18.

rows.notes: Most felonies must be charged within 5 years. Exceptions: no limit for capital offenses, felonies involving violence, serious injury or death, sex offenses against victims under 16, arson, forgery, counterfeiting and drug trafficking.

Most felonies must be charged within 5 years. Exceptions: no limit for murder, kidnapping, felony sexual abuse of a minor and serious sexual assault; 10 years for felony manslaughter, assault, stalking and certain other crimes against the person.

Class 2 through 6 felonies must be charged within 7 years after the offense is discovered (or should have been). No limit for homicide, violent sexual assault, class 2 sex offenses, misuse of public money and certain other crimes.
rows.issue: The old note implied different periods by felony class; 7 years applies to all class 2-6 felonies, measured from discovery.

rows.notes: Class B, C, D and unclassified felonies must be charged within 3 years; Class Y and Class A felonies within 6 years. No limit for capital murder, first- and second-degree murder and listed sex offenses against minors.

Most felonies must be charged within 3 years. Exceptions: 6 years for felonies punishable by 8 or more years in prison, and no limit for crimes punishable by death or life and for many felony sex offenses.
Most felonies must be charged within 3 years. No limit for murder, kidnapping, treason, sex offenses against children and forgery; 20 years for felony sexual assault of an adult.
rows.issue: The old note wrongly said class 4-5 felonies have no limit; the 3-year period applies to ordinary felonies of every class.

rows.notes: Offenses punishable by more than one year in prison must be charged within 5 years. No limit for class A felonies and sex offenses against minors; 20 years for most felony sexual assaults of adults.
Most felonies must be charged within 5 years. No limit for murder and any class A felony (and sex offenses against minors); a lapsed case can still be brought within 10 years if based on DNA testing.

Most felonies must be charged within 6 years. No limit for murder and for first- through fourth-degree sexual abuse, child sexual abuse and incest; 10 years for certain trafficking and child-exploitation crimes.
Second- and third-degree felonies must be charged within 3 years and first-degree felonies within 4 years. No limit for capital felonies, life felonies and felonies that caused a death.
Most felonies must be charged within 4 years (7 years if the victim was under 18). Other crimes punishable by death or life have 7 years, forcible rape 15 years, and murder has no limit.
Class B and C felonies must be charged within 3 years and class A felonies within 6 years. No limit for murder, attempted murder and first- and second-degree sexual assault.
Most felonies must be charged within 5 years. No limit for murder, voluntary manslaughter, most forcible rape, sexual abuse or lewd conduct with a child, and terrorism.

Most felonies must be charged within 3 years. No limit for murder, manslaughter, reckless homicide, arson, forgery, fatal DUI and offenses involving sexual conduct or penetration; Section 3-6 extends other crimes.
rows.issue: The old note wrongly said Class X and Class 1 felonies have no limit; they are covered by the 3-year rule unless a listed exception applies.

rows.notes: Level 3 to Level 6 felonies must be charged within 5 years. Level 1 and Level 2 felonies and murder can be charged at any time.

Most felonies must be charged within 3 years. Exceptions: no limit for murder and for serious sexual abuse of a minor; 10 years for other first- to third-degree sexual abuse; other special periods for kidnapping, trafficking and robbery.
Most crimes must be charged within 5 years. No limit for murder, rape, aggravated criminal sodomy and terrorism; 10 years (or 1 year after DNA identification) for other sexually violent crimes.
Kentucky has no time limit for any felony unless a statute expressly provides one.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years; Kentucky felonies have no statute of limitations.

rows.notes: Felonies necessarily punishable at hard labor must be charged within 6 years; other felonies within 4 years. No limit for crimes punishable by death or life, second-degree rape and molestation of a juvenile.
rows.issue: The old note gave only 6 years; felonies not necessarily punishable at hard labor have 4 years.

rows.notes: Maine uses crime classes instead of 'felony'; Class A, B and C crimes must be charged within 6 years. No limit for murder and for sex crimes against minors; 20 years for Class A-C gross sexual assault and unlawful sexual contact.
Maryland has no time limit for felonies. The 1-year limit and its listed exceptions apply only to misdemeanors.
Most crimes must be charged within 6 years. Exceptions: no limit for murder and listed sex crimes against children; 15 years for rape; 10 years for armed robbery and certain other crimes.
Most crimes must be charged within 6 years. No limit for murder and first-degree criminal sexual conduct; longer periods for second- and third-degree criminal sexual conduct and other listed crimes.

Most crimes must be charged within 3 years. No limit for crimes causing death and first- to fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct; longer periods apply to some financial crimes, arson and trafficking.
rows.issue: The old note said class 2 felonies have 6 years; Minnesota has no felony classes, and the 3-year catch-all applies.

rows.notes: Felonies not on the no-limit list must be charged within 2 years. The no-limit list is long: murder, manslaughter, aggravated assault, kidnapping, arson, burglary, robbery, rape, larceny, embezzlement and more.
Most felonies must be charged within 3 years. No limit for murder, first-degree and forcible rape and sodomy, and any class A felony; 5 years for certain arson crimes.
rows.issue: The old note said class B felonies have no limit; only class A felonies and listed offenses do.

rows.notes: Most felonies must be charged within 5 years. No limit for deliberate, mitigated and negligent homicide; 10 years for listed sex crimes (no limit if the victim was under 18).
Misdemeanors must be charged within 12 months.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 5 years, the same period as most felonies.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 1 year after discovery; petty offenses within 6 months. DUI has its own 2-year period.
Misdemeanors and violations must be charged within 1 year.
Most misdemeanors must be charged within 1 year; some listed misdemeanors have longer periods.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 18 months; class 1 and 2 misdemeanor traffic offenses within 1 year, petty offenses within 6 months.
Offenses punishable by one year or less must be charged within 1 year.
Class B, class C and unclassified misdemeanors must be charged within 2 years; class A misdemeanors within 3 years.
Non-felony offenses must be charged within 3 years.
First-degree misdemeanors must be charged within 2 years; second-degree misdemeanors within 1 year.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 2 years.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 2 years; petty misdemeanors and violations within 1 year.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 1 year.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 18 months unless the statute for the offense says otherwise.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 2 years.
Aggravated and serious misdemeanors must be charged within 3 years; simple misdemeanors within 1 year.
Kansas uses one 5-year period for most crimes, misdemeanors included.
rows.issue: Value was 2 years; the 2-year period was replaced by 5 years for all crimes not otherwise listed.

rows.notes: Misdemeanors and violations must be charged within 1 year.
Misdemeanors punishable by jail must be charged within 2 years; fine-only misdemeanors within 6 months.
Class D and E crimes (Maine's misdemeanors) must be charged within 3 years.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 1 year. Major exception: a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment in the penitentiary can be charged at any time, and some listed offenses have 2-3 years.
Massachusetts uses one 6-year period for most crimes, misdemeanors included.
Michigan uses one 6-year period for most crimes, misdemeanors included.
Minnesota uses one 3-year period for most crimes, misdemeanors included.
Offenses not on the no-limit list, misdemeanors included, must be charged within 2 years.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 1 year; infractions within 6 months.
Misdemeanors must be charged within 1 year.
A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 1 year; a felony DUI (for example, one causing injury) falls under the felony periods.
rows.issue: Value was 3 years, the felony-DUI period; the misdemeanor DUI period is 1 year.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 2 years if treated as a first-degree misdemeanor or 1 year if second-degree; felony DUI has 3 years.
rows.issue: The value of 3 years is the felony-DUI period. We could not read the statute that sets which misdemeanor degree DUI counts as, so the 1- or 2-year period is unconfirmed.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 12 months, like other misdemeanors.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years (the felony period); misdemeanors have 12 months.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 5 years, the general period for most offenses.
A DUI must be charged within 2 years after it is actually discovered, longer than the 1-year rule for other misdemeanors.
rows.citation: Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 13-107(B), 28-1381 (as amended by 2023 S.B. 1085)
rows.issue: Value was 1 year; a 2023 law gave DUI under § 28-1381 its own 2-year period.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DWI must be charged within 1 year, like other misdemeanors.
A misdemeanor DUI falls under either the 18-month misdemeanor period or the 1-year period for class 1 and 2 misdemeanor traffic offenses, depending on how DUI is classified.
rows.issue: The value of 5 years is wrong (no Colorado misdemeanor period is that long), but the page we read does not say whether DUI is a class 1/2 misdemeanor traffic offense (1 year) or a general misdemeanor (18 months).

rows.notes: A first-offense DUI (up to 6 months in jail) must be charged within 1 year. A repeat DUI punishable by more than a year falls under the 5-year period.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years, which applies only to offenses punishable by more than one year.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 3 years, like other non-felony offenses.
A misdemeanor DUI, which is unclassified, must be charged within 2 years.
A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 2 years, like other misdemeanors.
rows.issue: Value was 4 years (the felony period); misdemeanors have 2 years.

rows.notes: Hawaii allows 2 years for misdemeanors and 1 year for petty misdemeanors; the period for a first OVUII depends on which class it is.
rows.issue: We could not read the statute that classifies a first OVUII (Haw. Rev. Stat. § 291E-61). If it is a petty misdemeanor the period is 1 year, not 2.

rows.notes: A first OWI is a serious misdemeanor and must be charged within 3 years.
A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 1 year, like other misdemeanors.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years (the felony period); misdemeanors have 1 year.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 18 months. Aggravated DUI that caused a death can be charged at any time.
rows.issue: Value was 18 years; the correct period is 18 months.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor OWI must be charged within 2 years, like other misdemeanors.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years (the felony period); misdemeanors have 2 years.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 5 years, the general Kansas period for most crimes.
A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 1 year, like other non-felony offenses.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years; Kentucky non-felony offenses have 1 year.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DWI, which is punishable by jail, must be charged within 2 years.
rows.issue: Value was 4 years (the period for some felonies); misdemeanors punishable by jail have 2 years.

rows.notes: An OUI must be charged within 6 years, the general Massachusetts period.
A DUI or DWI under Transportation § 21-902 is a misdemeanor with no special period, so it must be charged within 1 year.
rows.issue: Value was 'no limit'; § 5-106 lists no special period for § 21-902, so the 1-year misdemeanor rule applies.

rows.notes: A first OUI is a Class D crime and must be charged within 3 years.
rows.issue: Value was 6 years (the Class A-C period); Class D crimes have 3 years.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor OWI must be charged within 6 years, the general Michigan period.
A misdemeanor DWI must be charged within 3 years, the general Minnesota period.
A misdemeanor DWI must be charged within 1 year, like other misdemeanors.
rows.issue: Value was 3 years (the felony period); misdemeanors have 1 year.

rows.notes: A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 2 years, the general Mississippi period.
A misdemeanor DUI must be charged within 1 year, like other misdemeanors.
rows.issue: Value was 5 years (the felony period); misdemeanors have 1 year.
